section.title: The Idols of Babylon Fall
section.sectionRationale: This chapter draws the polemic against idolatry to its sharpest picture yet: Babylon's own gods, Bel and Nebo, become dead weight loaded onto exhausted animals in a desperate escape, while the LORD declares that He alone has carried Israel from the womb and will carry them still to old age. It presses home the Book of Comfort's central claim, that only the LORD declares the end from the beginning and His purpose cannot be stopped.
section.thesis: Babylon's idols must be carried away as dead weight by animals that stagger under their burden, but the LORD has carried Israel from the womb and promises to carry them to old age, because He alone declares the end from the beginning and no one can prevent His purpose from standing.
section.frameNote: Five movements: Babylon's gods collapse and are hauled away; the LORD's contrasting promise to carry His people from birth to old age; the folly of comparing God to a crafted idol; the LORD's declaration that His purpose will stand, unlike anything the idols can foretell; and the closing call for stubborn hearts to remember and draw near to His righteousness.

verses.text: Bel crouches; Nebo cowers. Their idols weigh down beasts and cattle. The images you carry are burdensome, a load to the weary animal.
The gods cower; they crouch together, unable to relieve the burden; but they themselves go into captivity.

units.label: I have carried you since birth

verses.text: “Listen to Me, O house of Jacob, all the remnant of the house of Israel, who have been sustained from the womb, carried along since birth.
Even to your old age, I will be the same, and I will bear you up when you turn gray. I have made you, and I will {{nasa|carry}} you; I will sustain you and deliver you.

units.label: To whom will you liken Me?

verses.text: To whom will you liken Me or count Me equal? To whom will you compare Me, that we should be alike?
They pour out their bags of gold and weigh out silver on scales; they hire a goldsmith to fashion it into a god, so they can bow down and worship.

They lift it to their shoulder and carry it along; they set it in its place, and there it stands, not budging from that spot. They cry out to it, but it does not answer; it saves no one from his troubles.

units.label: My purpose will stand
units.note: declaring the end from the beginning

verses.text: Remember this and be brave; take it to heart, you transgressors!
Remember what happened long ago, for I am God, and there is no other; I am God, and there is none like Me.
I declare the end from the beginning, and ancient times from what is still to come. I say, ‘My {{etsah|purpose}} will stand, and all My good pleasure I will accomplish.’
I summon a bird of prey from the east, a man for My purpose from a far-off land. Truly I have spoken, and truly I will bring it to pass. I have planned it, and I will surely do it.
Listen to Me, you stubborn people, far removed from righteousness:
I am bringing My righteousness near; it is not far away, and My salvation will not be delayed. I will grant salvation to Zion and adorn Israel with My splendor.

nasa.gloss: To carry, lift, bear, or bear up. The chapter's whole argument turns on this word: Babylon's idols must be carried as dead weight by exhausted animals, while the LORD carries His own people from the womb to old age, bearing their weight rather than being borne, a contrast that anticipates the ultimate bearing of sin itself at the cross, 1 Peter 2:24.

etsah.gloss: Counsel, purpose, or plan, the settled intention behind a course of action. The LORD's declaration that His etsah will stand is the theological center of the chapter, and indeed of the whole Book of Comfort: no idol, no empire, and no circumstance can prevent God's declared purpose from being accomplished exactly as He has spoken.

basic.context: This chapter pictures Babylon's chief gods, Bel and Nebo, being loaded like dead weight onto exhausted pack animals as their city falls, unable even to save themselves, let alone their worshipers. Against that image the LORD reminds Israel that He has carried them from the womb and will carry them still into old age, because He alone declares the future and His purpose cannot be stopped by anyone.
basic.hermeneutics: The vivid image of idols becoming a burden rather than a help exposes the core absurdity Isaiah has been building across these chapters: an idol must be carried, while the true God carries. The chapter's declaration in verse 10, that the LORD declares the end from the beginning, is the theological anchor for the whole Book of Comfort's confidence that God's promises, including the naming of Cyrus in the previous chapter, will certainly come to pass.
basic.originalLanguages: The whole chapter turns on the contrast built into {{nasa}}, to carry, since Babylon's idols must be carried as burdensome weight while the LORD promises to carry His people from birth to old age. That promise rests on His {{etsah}}, purpose or counsel, declared unshakeable, standing firm against every rival claim to control the future.
basic.typology: The LORD who carries His people rather than needing to be carried anticipates Christ, who does not merely sustain His people from a distance but takes on flesh to personally bear their sins in His own body, 1 Peter 2:24. The declaration that God's purpose will stand and His good pleasure will be accomplished, verse 10, anticipates the certainty of God's redemptive plan fulfilled in Christ, unshaken by any human or demonic opposition.
basic.christ: The contrast between idols that must be carried and the LORD who carries His people finds its deepest fulfillment in Christ, who 'Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree,' 1 Peter 2:24, carrying not merely His people's weight through life but the very weight of their sin at the cross. The declaration that God's purpose will stand and His good pleasure will be accomplished, verse 10, is the same confidence Paul expresses regarding God's eternal plan centered in Christ, Ephesians 1:11.
basic.god: God alone is able to carry His people rather than needing to be carried, sustaining them from the womb to old age with the same faithfulness across a whole lifetime. His purpose cannot be stopped by any rival power, human or supposedly divine, because He alone declares the end from the beginning and brings to pass exactly what He has spoken.
basic.crossReferences: Deuteronomy 32:11-12 pictures the LORD carrying Israel like an eagle bearing its young, similar carrying imagery. 1 Peter 2:24 describes Christ bearing our sins in His own body on the cross. Ephesians 1:11 affirms that God works all things according to the purpose of His will. Acts 15:18 declares that all God's works have been known to Him from eternity.
basic.oneStory: This chapter's contrast between burdensome idols and the God who carries His people traces the whole Bible's story of a God who does not merely watch from a distance but personally sustains and ultimately rescues His people. That carrying finds its deepest expression in Christ, who bore the full weight of sin itself, fulfilling the unstoppable purpose this chapter declares God will accomplish.

context.literary:
Isaiah 46 is written to be read beside chapter 47. Chapter 46 brings Babylon's gods down, chapter 47 brings Babylon's throne down, and together they are the climax of the long argument against idols that began in Isaiah 40:18-20 and was sharpened in the workshop satire of Isaiah 44:9-20. The chapter has a clear four part shape. Verses 1 and 2 are a scene told in the third person, with Israel standing at the roadside and watching. Verses 3 to 4 turn to address the exiles directly, and verses 5 to 7 return to the idols in a mocking parody of an ordinary day in the shop. Verses 8 to 13 then gather everything into a summons.

The whole chapter is held together by one repeated idea, carrying. The idols are 'carried' in verse 1, Israel has been 'carried along since birth' in verse 3, the LORD says 'I will carry you' in verse 4, and the craftsman's god is lifted to the shoulder and carried in verse 7. The first and last carrying frame the middle two, so that the reader is made to watch the same action done in opposite directions. Worshipers carry gods; the God of Jacob carries worshipers.

The chapter is also cut by two summonses with the same opening, 'Listen to Me,' in verse 3 to the faithful remnant and in verse 12 to the stubborn. Between them sit two commands to remember, in verses 8 and 9. The first group is comforted, the second is confronted, and the same God speaks to both.
context.historical:
Bel is a title meaning 'lord,' and Jeremiah uses it as another name for Marduk, the patron god of the city, Jeremiah 50:2 and 51:44. Nebo, in the Babylonian pantheon Nabu, was linked with writing and with scribal wisdom and was honoured as the son of Marduk. Ancient Mesopotamians did not think of such images as mere statues. The image was washed, clothed, fed and carried out in procession on festival days, and Babylon's great spring festival centred on parading the gods through the streets. Isaiah takes this very pageantry and turns it upside down. In his scene the procession becomes a retreat, and the gods are loaded on carts and animals like household goods.

There was a hard political reality behind it. In the ancient Near East a defeated people's gods were routinely seized and carted off as plunder, which is how a conqueror announced that the gods had lost. Babylon had carried off Judah's temple vessels, 2 Chronicles 36:18. Isaiah promises the reverse, that Babylon's gods will be the captives.

The fall itself came in 539 BC when Cyrus of Persia entered Babylon, and the Babylonian records suggest the city yielded with little fighting. Isaiah does not describe a battle; he describes the humiliation of gods whose city has fallen. The Judeans who first heard this lived among these processions in a land where the visible evidence seemed to say that Marduk had conquered the LORD. Isaiah 46 is God's answer to that evidence, and it was spoken for people whose faith was being tested by what they saw each day.
context.canonical:
The chapter belongs to a long line of passages that picture God as a carrier. In the wilderness He bore Israel like an eagle bearing its young, Deuteronomy 32:11-12, and Hosea remembers Him teaching Ephraim to walk and taking them in His arms, Hosea 11:3-4. Later in Isaiah the same picture returns when the book looks back on the exodus: 'He lifted them up and carried them all the days of old,' Isaiah 63:9. Isaiah 40:11 says the Shepherd carries the lambs close to His heart, so that Isaiah 46:3-4 belongs to the Book of Comfort's central image of a gentle, strong God.

The line about old age is taken up in the psalms of the aged, where a believer prays that God would not forsake him when he is old and gray, Psalm 71:17-18. The mockery of the idol is picked up again in Jeremiah 10:3-5, in Paul's address in Athens, 'we should not think that the Divine Being is like gold or silver or stone,' Acts 17:29, and in Romans 1:22-23, where Paul says humanity exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images.

The statement that God's purpose stands is echoed in the New Testament. In Acts 15:17-18 the Jerusalem council reads God's saving of the Gentiles as something 'known for ages,' and Ephesians 1:11 speaks of God working out everything by the counsel of His will. The promise that salvation will not be delayed, verse 13, is taken up in the gospel language of righteousness brought near, Romans 3:21-22. The chapter also stands at the hinge of Isaiah's second part, before the Servant material of chapters 49 to 53 shows how this nearness of salvation comes about.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Isaiah wants the exiles to see two things about their situation that the evidence on the ground would hide. The first is that the gods of the conqueror are not strong. Verse 2 says they are 'unable to relieve the burden,' meaning they cannot rescue even themselves, and verse 7 says the idol 'saves no one from his troubles.' The prophet does not argue philosophically that such gods are impossible; he shows what they do, which is nothing, and lets the picture speak.

The second is that the God of Israel has been carrying them the whole time. Verse 3 reaches back to the womb, and verse 4 reaches forward to grey hair. The exiles had probably read their captivity as proof that they had been dropped. Isaiah says the arms underneath them were never withdrawn, and that the arms belong to the same God who made them, 'I have made you, and I will carry you.'

He also wanted the stubborn among them to stop and think. Verses 8 and 12 are sharp words to people who half believed the promises and half preferred the comfortable idols of Babylon. They are told to remember what happened long ago, because God's record is long and the idols have none. The chapter ends with an offer rather than a threat, since God says His righteousness is near and His salvation will not wait.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: The chapter describes Babylon's idols and what happens to them; it does not give orders about statues, temples or festivals, and it should not be turned into a general rule about carrying burdens. The command element is small and aimed at Israel: listen, remember, take it to heart, verses 3, 8, 9 and 12. The mockery of the craftsman in verses 6 and 7 is a satire written for the faithful remnant. It is not a model for how believers speak to a neighbour who prays to an image today, and Paul himself speaks with respect and care in Athens, Acts 17:22-29.\n\nThe promise that God will carry His people to old age is a promise to the people of God as a body, and it is steady and firm. It is not a guarantee that a believer will never be weary, ill or poor in old age. The same Bible includes the old man's prayer, 'do not forsake me,' Psalm 71:18, and the pain of those who grow weak. What the text affirms is that God does not let go. Application should rest on His presence and His character rather than on a promise of ease. The verb 'carry' in the chapter also sets a quiet test for any modern idol. If a thing has to be carried, maintained and propped up by us in order to keep working, it is not the God who carries.

debates.question: Does 'My purpose will stand, and all My good pleasure I will accomplish,' verse 10, describe God's control over every individual event, or the certainty of His overall plan?

views.label: Comprehensive sovereignty over every detail
views.case: The sentence sits beside Isaiah 45:7, where the LORD says He forms light and creates darkness, and beside the word of Ephesians 1:11 that God 'works out everything by the counsel of His will.' On this reading the chapter excludes any part of history from His purpose. The pairing of 'end' and 'beginning' in verse 10 seems to include the whole run of events between them.

views.label: A certain overall purpose, with God working through real human choices
views.case: The verse names a particular purpose, the fall of Babylon and the rescue of Israel, and says nothing about explaining every event. Elsewhere Isaiah holds God's purpose together with human responsibility, since Israel is called 'stubborn' in verse 12 and is told to turn. These readers say the text guarantees God's plan without describing the way each detail is caused.

debates.bearing: Both views agree on what the text most needs to say: no rival can overturn what God has declared, and the exiles can build their hope on it. The debate about mechanism is real, but verse 12 shows that the chapter itself calls on the stubborn to listen, which means the promise is meant to move people, not to excuse them.

debates.question: When was this prophecy written, and does that change its argument about foretelling?

views.label: Isaiah of Jerusalem, speaking beforehand
views.case: The book names Isaiah as the prophet of the eighth century and Cyrus appears by name in Isaiah 44:28 and 45:1. On this view the force of verse 10 is literal, since the LORD declares the end from the beginning and the naming of a conqueror generations ahead is the very proof that no idol could give.

views.label: A prophet in the exile, speaking to the exiles
views.case: Many scholars read chapters 40 to 55 as addressed to people already in Babylon on the eve of Cyrus's rise, because the audience, the images and the Babylonian detail all fit that setting. On this view the verses claim that God's word has been proved true in the past, in Israel's history, and offer the coming of 'a bird of prey from the east' as the next proof.

debates.bearing: The argument of the chapter survives either way. God's claim is that He alone can say what will happen and then make it happen, so the God who spoke earlier prophecies and fulfilled them can be trusted for this one. Readers should state which view they hold and then notice that Isaiah himself asks his hearers to remember the long record, verse 9, rather than to trust one isolated forecast.

study.originalLanguages:
Two verbs of carrying are used in the chapter and they are worth telling apart. The verb nasa is the common Hebrew word for lifting and bearing. It describes the idol carriers in verse 1, and it is the verb in the LORD's promise in verse 4, 'I will carry you.' It also means to forgive, since God 'lifts' sin, and that second range of meaning stands quietly behind the promise. Verse 4 pairs it with sabal, to bear a heavy load. Isaiah uses that same verb of the Servant in Isaiah 53:4, who has borne our sorrows, so the God who here says He will carry is, by the book's own vocabulary, the God who takes weight on Himself. The three-fold statement of verse 4, 'I have made you, and I will carry you; I will sustain you and deliver you,' lists the Maker, the Bearer and the Rescuer in one breath.

The opening of verse 4 has no verb at all. Where the BSB reads 'I will be the same,' the Hebrew simply says 'to old age, I am He,' using the bare pronouns that carry the divine self declaration in Isaiah 41:4, 43:10 and 43:13. It is the claim to eternity expressed in the smallest possible way. Before the verse says what God will do, it says what He is, and the doing follows from the being.

The 'bird of prey' of verse 11 is a word for a swooping raptor that picks out the speed of Cyrus's advance from the east. Isaiah 41:25 describes the same coming from the east and north. The phrase translated 'a man for My purpose' is literally 'a man of My counsel,' using the same noun, etsah, as in verse 10. The conqueror is described not as an independent king but as an instrument of God's counsel. The two repeated verbs of verse 11, 'Truly I have spoken, and truly I will bring it to pass. I have planned it, and I will surely do it,' pair a verb of saying with a verb of doing and close the gap between them.

The phrase for 'stubborn people' in verse 12 is literally those 'strong of heart.' In English that sounds like praise, but here it names obstinacy, a heart so strong that it will not bend toward righteousness. It is set against the word for righteousness in verse 13, tsedaqah, which is said to be brought near, together with salvation, teshuah. In Isaiah righteousness and salvation are close companions, and the pair here is a gift that comes toward the people and does not wait for them to climb to it.

The 'I declare' of verse 10 comes from a verb meaning to tell or announce, so God is presented as the one who reports the future before it happens, which is exactly the thing Isaiah says no idol can do.

typology.type: The idol carried and the God who carries
typology.fulfillment: The picture of a god that has to be lifted by tired beasts finds its opposite in the incarnation. The LORD who promises to bear His people does not do it from a distance. The Son 'bore our sins in His body on the tree,' 1 Peter 2:24, and He invites the weary, 'Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened,' Matthew 11:28. The escalation is that the load is no longer only tiredness and age but guilt itself. The type falls short only in that Isaiah's carrying is a promise of presence, while Christ's carrying includes substitution.

The sight of powerless gods marched away anticipates the way Christ disarms the hostile powers, Colossians 2:15, and the unmasking of the powers behind idols. The pattern is that the visible order which seemed to be in control is revealed to be a captive. The fulfilment is deeper, since Christ does not merely expose false gods but brings the people they held into freedom. The type is limited because Isaiah describes the fall of a city, and the final judgment of every false power waits for the end, Revelation 18.

typology.type: The bird of prey from the east, God's chosen instrument
typology.fulfillment: Cyrus is raised up from far away to carry out God's purpose, so that a foreign king serves the saving plan without knowing the God he serves, Isaiah 45:4. He is a shadow of the way God uses outsiders to bring rescue, and he is called 'anointed,' Isaiah 45:1, the same word that gives the Messiah His title. The escalation is that Cyrus releases a people from a city, while Jesus releases people from sin and death and is the Anointed in His own right. The type breaks down because Cyrus acted without knowing the LORD, Isaiah 45:4, and was never more than an instrument.

typology.type: Righteousness brought near, salvation not delayed
typology.fulfillment: The promise of verse 13 is the Old Testament form of what Paul calls the righteousness of God 'apart from the law,' Romans 3:21-22, brought near in Christ. In Isaiah it comes as a rescue of Zion from Babylon, and in the gospel it comes as a righteousness that is received through faith in Jesus Christ. The fulfilment goes further than the type because it reaches Jew and Gentile alike. The type is partial in that the return from Babylon did not end exile in the fuller sense, and the book itself keeps looking ahead.

study.christ:
The chapter points to Christ first by contrast between the carried and the carrier. Babylon's gods have to be lifted onto beasts; Jesus is the Son 'upholding all things by His powerful word,' Hebrews 1:3. The verb in Isaiah 46:4 becomes flesh and blood when the Shepherd takes the weight on His own shoulders. He opens His arms to every burdened person, Matthew 11:28-30, and calls His own yoke easy and His burden light, which is how a carrier speaks to those who cannot go on.

It points to Christ also by way of the promise of verse 4, 'I will be the same.' Hebrews 13:8 says 'Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.' The writer is not quoting Isaiah, but the idea is the same: the God who does not change in old age has not changed in the person of His Son. The title 'the first and the last,' which Isaiah 44:6 and 48:12 give to the LORD, is spoken by the risen Christ of Himself in Revelation 1:17 and 22:13, so the Creator who declares the end from the beginning is the one who walks among His churches.

The 'man for My purpose' from the east is a type of deliverance, and the New Testament shows how Christ outranks every such deliverer. Cyrus freed a people from a city, and Christ frees people from the dominion of darkness. Isaiah's 'My righteousness near' and Paul's righteousness of God apart from the law, Romans 3:21-22, are two sides of one hope. In the cross the righteousness that was far off, the thing stubborn people could not reach, is brought to them in a person.

A word of care. The chapter does not secretly name Jesus, and it would be wrong to read the idols as veiled pictures of Satan or the carts as hints of the cross. The links rest on the biblical themes of carrying, of God's unchanged character and of righteousness brought near, and on the way the New Testament itself picks them up. What the chapter supplies is the conviction that the God who rescues is not a God who needs help, and what the gospel supplies is the face and the wounds of the one who carries.
study.god:
The chapter first shows a God who is utterly self sufficient. Babylon's gods depend on porters, carts and craftsmen; they were made by the people who serve them, verse 6. The LORD says that He made Israel, verse 4, and that He needs no one to carry Him. The difference between the Creator and everything created is the hinge of the whole argument. He cannot be compared, verse 5, because comparison needs two things on the same level, and there is no second thing on His level.

It shows a God who is faithful over time. The promise spans a whole life, from birth to grey hair, and it is expressed as sameness, 'I will be the same.' Doctrine calls this immutability, and here it is not cold distance but the reliability of a person. He does not tire of those He has made. The God who made them is the God who sustains them, so that creation and care are one work.

It shows a God who knows and governs the future. Verse 10 says He declares the end from the beginning, and verse 11 gives the example, the raising up of Cyrus. This is both foreknowledge and purpose. The two verbs in verse 11, 'I have planned it' and 'I will surely do it,' belong together. The chapter does not say that God merely sees what is coming; it says that He plans it and carries it out.

It shows a God who is both patient and urgent. The stubborn are not struck down in verse 12; they are addressed. Verse 13 says that righteousness and salvation are close, and the promise that salvation 'will not be delayed' reveals a God who is neither slow nor rash. He has the whole timeline in view, yet He moves toward His people with real warmth, speaking to them as 'house of Jacob.'

There is a tension worth holding. God is sovereign enough to use a pagan king, yet He remains the one who is 'bringing My righteousness near' to a people who do not deserve it. Isaiah does not resolve this by reducing either side. For worship the lesson is that we do not bring God anything He lacks. Praise in this chapter is the response of those who have been carried, and trust is the proper answer to a God who has never dropped anyone He made.

crossReferences.note: The eagle hovering over its young and carrying them on its pinions is the oldest picture behind verses 3 and 4. Moses adds that the LORD alone led Israel and no foreign god was with him. Isaiah says the same thing to people now living among foreign gods, reminding them of the way they came out of Egypt.

The first mockery of the idol in the Book of Comfort. A craftsman casts it, a metalworker overlays it, and a skilled man sets it up so that it will not topple. Chapter 46 takes up the same image and finishes it with the idol standing in its place, unable to move, verse 7.

The long workshop satire in which the same wood warms the man, cooks his food and becomes his god. It prepares the ground for 46:6-7, where the idol is bought, set up and prayed to, and answers no prayer. Isaiah says the idol maker cannot see that he holds a lie in his right hand.

A prophet of the fall of Babylon who names Bel and Marduk together, in the same language of shame as Isaiah 46:1. Jeremiah shows that the humiliation of the gods is part of what Babylon's fall means, which confirms the historical reading of Isaiah's scene.

Looking back at the exodus, the book says that in all their distress the LORD was afflicted, that the Angel of His Presence saved them and that He 'carried them all the days of old.' The promise of 46:4 is thereby shown to be His settled way of dealing with Israel and not a passing mood.

An old believer who has been taught by God from youth prays not to be forsaken when he is old and gray. It is a personal echo of Isaiah 46:4, showing how the promise was taken into prayer and how ordinary believers used it to face the weakness of age.

Where the 'man for My purpose' of 46:11 is named as Cyrus. God calls him by name, and calls him His anointed, for the sake of Jacob, though Cyrus has not known Him. The earlier chapter gives the name that the later one only hints at.

God's word that goes out from His mouth does not come back empty but accomplishes what He pleases. It is the same confidence as 46:10-11, 'I have spoken, and truly I will bring it to pass,' and shows that the Book of Comfort holds one unified view of the power of God's word.

Paul argues in Athens that if we are God's offspring we should not think the Divine Being is like gold or silver or stone. It is the apostolic form of Isaiah 46:5-7, taking the prophet's argument about the made and the Maker into the Greek world.

Paul says believers were chosen according to the plan of Him who works out everything by the counsel of His will. It is the New Testament statement of Isaiah 46:10, in which God's purpose stands, and it places the believer inside that purpose as one who has been chosen.

study.oneStory:
The chapter answers an old question in Scripture, which is who really rules the nations. Genesis 11 shows the people of Babel building toward the heavens to make a name for themselves, and the name Babel becomes the Bible's shorthand for human pride organised against God. Isaiah 46 is the stage at which that long story reaches the actual city. Its gods are loaded up like freight, its power is turned to rubble, and the people it enslaved are told that they have been carried the whole time.

The chapter also looks back. The exodus, where God carried Israel on eagles' wings and brought them out from under Pharaoh and the gods of Egypt, is the pattern, and Isaiah treats the return from Babylon as a second exodus. As Egypt's gods were judged in the first, so Babylon's are shamed in the second, and in each case the people are carried out by a God who needs no help.

It looks forward as well. The words 'My salvation will not be delayed,' verse 13, are fulfilled in stages. They are fulfilled in 539 BC when Cyrus lets the people go, they are fulfilled more fully when the Servant brings salvation to the ends of the earth in the chapters just ahead, and they are fulfilled at the cross and resurrection, where the God who bears His people takes up their sin. The Bible does not leave the story with idols dismantled; it ends with Babylon fallen for good, Revelation 18, and with a people carried safely home.

In the new creation the final scene of chapter 46 is reversed in the best way. There are no more processions of burdened beasts, no more gods that cannot answer, and no more weary porters. The people who were carried from the womb to old age are met by the one who carried them, and they see His face, Revelation 22:4. The promise 'I will be the same' holds to the end, because the Lamb who is the first and the last is also the one who will wipe every tear from their eyes, Revelation 21:4.

quiz.q: What happens to Babylon's gods, Bel and Nebo, in verses 1 to 2?

options.text: They become a burdensome load carried by exhausted animals and are themselves taken into captivity.
options.note: Verses 1 to 2 describe exactly this humiliating scene of idols needing rescue rather than providing it.

options.text: They successfully defend Babylon from all attackers.
options.note: The opposite; the idols collapse and must be evacuated, unable to save the city or themselves.

options.text: They are worshiped with even greater devotion after this event.
options.note: The passage depicts humiliation and captivity for these idols, not increased devotion.

options.text: They are melted down and used to build new temples.
options.note: The text describes them being carried away as a burden into captivity, not repurposed for new temples.

quiz.q: What contrasting promise does the LORD make about Israel in verses 3 to 4?

options.text: He has carried them from the womb and will bear them up even to old age.
options.note: Verses 3 to 4 state this promise directly, contrasting with the idols that must be carried.

options.text: He will abandon them once they reach old age.
options.note: The opposite; the promise explicitly extends His carrying to old age and beyond.

options.text: He requires Israel to carry Him, just as Babylon carries its idols.
options.note: The whole point of the contrast is that the LORD carries His people, unlike idols that must be carried.

options.text: He will only help Israel if they first prove their strength.
options.note: The promise is unconditional care from the womb onward, not contingent on Israel's own strength.

quiz.q: What does verse 7 say about an idol's ability to respond to those who cry out to it?

options.text: It does not answer and saves no one from his troubles.
options.note: Verse 7 states this directly, the core indictment against idol worship.

options.text: It answers immediately and rescues its worshipers.
options.note: The opposite; the text emphasizes the idol's total inability to answer or save.

options.text: It answers only the wealthiest worshipers.
options.note: The text describes total inability to answer anyone, not selective responsiveness based on wealth.

options.text: It answers only after elaborate rituals are performed.
options.note: The text gives no indication of eventual response after ritual; it states the idol simply does not answer at all.

quiz.q: What does the LORD declare about Himself uniquely in verse 10?

options.text: He declares the end from the beginning, and His purpose will stand.
options.note: Verse 10 states this unique claim directly, central to the whole chapter's argument.

options.text: He is uncertain about the future, like the idols.
options.note: The opposite; He claims certain, comprehensive knowledge and control of the future, unlike any idol.

options.text: His plans frequently change and can be altered by other gods.
options.note: The verse specifically claims His purpose will stand, not that it is subject to change or alteration.

options.text: He only knows the past, not the future.
options.note: The claim explicitly includes declaring 'the end from the beginning,' encompassing the future, not only the past.

quiz.q: What does the LORD promise in the chapter's closing verse, verse 13?

options.text: He is bringing His righteousness near and His salvation will not be delayed, granting salvation to Zion.
options.note: Verse 13 gives exactly this closing promise of near, certain salvation.

options.text: Salvation will be indefinitely postponed with no clear timeline.
options.note: The opposite; the verse specifically says salvation 'will not be delayed.'

options.text: Only future generations will experience this promised salvation.
options.note: The language emphasizes nearness and lack of delay, not a promise deferred only to distant future generations.

options.text: Righteousness and salvation depend entirely on Israel's own effort.
options.note: The verse presents this as God's own initiative, 'I am bringing,' not something earned by Israel's effort.

questions: Babylon's idols became a burden that had to be carried, while the LORD carries His own people. What are you currently carrying, trying to manage or fix, that you need to let God carry instead?
God promises to sustain His people from the womb to old age, not just in youth or strength. How does this shape the way you think about aging, weakness, or seasons of life that feel less productive?
The idol in verse 7 cannot answer or save anyone who cries out to it. What do you turn to that, if you are honest, cannot actually answer you when you call?

God declares that His purpose will stand and nothing can stop it. What current uncertainty in your life do you need to entrust to that unshakeable purpose rather than trying to control the outcome yourself?
The chapter closes with the promise that God's salvation will not be delayed. Where do you need to trust God's timing rather than assuming He has forgotten or delayed His promises to you?

translationNotes.note: Bel, another name for Marduk, and Nebo, or Nabu, were principal deities of the Babylonian pantheon, making their humiliation here a direct challenge to Babylon's own religious confidence.

This verse, 'I declare the end from the beginning,' is the theological anchor for the whole Book of Comfort's confidence that God's specific promises, including the naming of Cyrus in the preceding chapters, will certainly be fulfilled.
'A bird of prey from the east' most likely continues the imagery applied to Cyrus in the surrounding chapters, a swift, decisive conqueror summoned by God for His own purposes.
